newsitem.title: NEPAL: FEATURE-Nepal's hardy Gurkhas bid HK farewell.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Nepal's hardy Gurkhas bid HK farewell.

text.p: A small but proud slice of Nepal will withdraw from Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to China in a few days.

Military emissaries for this landlocked Himalayan kingdom around the world, Gurkha soldiers have served in Hong Kong under British colours for nearly half a century. At one time more than 3,000 were stationed in Hong Kong.
Renowned for their loyalty and deadly fighting skills, the last Gurkha infantry battalion departed in October.
Now the few remaining Gurkhas -- drivers and signal specialists -- will be pulling out of Hong Kong to face an uncertain future as Britain reins in its defence commitments.
Dipak Bahadur Gurung served for 30 years in Hong Kong before retiring in 1989 as an army major.
"We went to night clubs during the weekend and enjoyed the night life in Hong Kong," he told Reuters in the Nepali capital. "This made the stay most exciting and enjoyable."
Gurung remembers when, as a border guard, he would see Chinese fleeing the mainland, either swimming to Hong Kong or vaulting the border fence.
"This showed how difficult life was in China compared with Hong Kong," he said. He later served as Queen Elizabeth's orderly, attending 150 cocktail parties in one year.
BROAD-BRIMMED HATS, CURVED DAGGERS

The stout and medium-built Gurkhas, of Mongolian origin from Nepal's Himalayan foothills, have served in the British army for 180 years. Some 232,000 fought under the British Crown in the two world wars.

British officials say more than 14,000 were killed and 28,000 wounded in those two wars, but ex-servicemen say many Wearing wide-brimmed hats and wielding curved daggers called "khukuris", Gurkhas served in the Falklands and the Gulf War.
"No, no, no, we are not mercenaries," Gurung says. "A 1947 treaty between Britain, India and Nepal recognises the Gurkhas as a regular part of the British army."
Many Gurkhas saw little more of Hong Kong than their barracks.

"It was not too bad," said 60-year old Ram Bahadur Limbu, who was only allowed into central Hong Kong on occasional weekends. "Life for a soldier was the same in the barracks whether it was in Hong Kong or in Britain."
The departure from Hong Kong is part of a longer trend that picked up pace with the end of the Cold War.

"The impact of the handover had already started being felt in Nepal in 1992 when Britain announced a cut in the number of Gurkhas in its army," said analyst and author Pratyoush Onta, who has studied the Gurkhas.
Britain has said Gurkhas will remain in its army, but their numbers will eventually be reduced to 2,500 from 3,900.
Nepal is concerned the cuts will worsen unemployment in the Hindu kingdom, one of the world's 10 poorest nations.
"The employment opportunities would decrease to the extent of the retrenchment of troops," former foreign minister Prakash Chandra Lohani said.
Gurkha remittances have become an important source of foreign exchange inflows for Nepal, increasing from 275.4 million rupees ($4.8 million) in 1985 to 1.84 billion rupees in 1995.
EQUAL SERVICE, EQUAL PAY

In February, in its first major review in 40 years of Gurkha terms of service, the British army announced Gurkha soldiers had won the right to bring their families with them to Britain under a one million pound ($1.6 million) package.
Gurkha officers and senior non-commissioned officers from Nepal who served in the British garrison in Hong Kong can have their families with them on a permanent basis.
Sergeants and junior soldiers receive "family permission" for at least three years during their first 15 years of service. Such "accompanied service" had not been permitted in Britain.
They will be able either to send their children to British schools or receive education allowances back home.
Britain also announced equal pay for Gurkha soldiers, bringing them in line with their British counterparts.
But in March, thousands of Gurkha soldiers demonstrated in Kathmandu, demanding pensions and other benefits on a par with their British counterparts.
"We are preparing to visit London as soon as possible for this," Padam Bahadur Gurung, president of the Gurkha Army Ex-Servicemen Organisation, told Reuters recently.
FROM DEFENCE TO TRADE
Some Gurkhas who have already pulled out of Hong Kong have been deployed to units in Britain.
Others have taken up civilian jobs in Hong Kong, become security guards in Brunei or returned to Nepal where they have little chance of finding a job.
Officials said Nepal's military liaison office in Hong Kong had been replaced by a consulate-general to tap trade and tourism.
Currently more than 25,000 Nepalis -- mostly ex-Gurkha soldiers and their children -- are working in Hong Kong, many in construction.
"China has assured us that it will let them continue to work there," said an ex-soldier in Kathmandu. ($1 = 57.1 Nepali rupees)
